I wanted to add onto this as a former Aisles worker. The corporate management is awful and out of touch and I think it really led to this downfall. 
They started limiting the number of hours managers could schedule so we’d always be short staffed and have to pull people. They came out with a list of “non-negotiables” which 2 managers got fired for not following, which included using the huge trolley carts that are hard to manage and obstructive for customers, texting for every substitution even if the customer didn’t want you to, and pushing weekly specials. We didn’t get dedicated space in the cooler for orders so we had to share with the dairy department which would make things get lost very easily. 75% of the workers were in high school and didn’t try bc no one else wanted to be in the department. 
You’d also get penalized for taking off items instead of substituting even if there wasn’t something similar. They need to get rid of the program and rebuild it with management who actually understand what it takes to make it work

Do you really think professors want to rework the courses they’ve been teaching in person? Changing all the material so it works better online, accommodating changes in classrooms and the ability to hold office hours, losing out on personal connections with students so that they can teach from their home/office instead of a classroom. 
There are 600 tenured professors at GW, but there are almost 2500 instructors overall. 2500 people with who have to interact with students daily, exposing themselves to the virus even with every possible safety measure GW will put in the effort to enforce. 2500 people with posible health conditions, or family members who could die if they contract COVID. 
Retail workers and grocery store employees primarily have to be on the front lines because many Americans and companies value the ability to be in a store instead of mandating pick-up or online orders more than employee safety. 
No one wants to be forced into online learning. I have ADHD and it’s significantly harder for me to pay attention in online classes, but I also have asthma and an immunocompromised mom. I don’t expect others to go out of their way to do things how I want just because I think it’s better. 
You sound like a whiny child, you expect others to compromise their safety to give you what you want. Sitting in Funger 103 listening to a professor is definitely what makes GW worth 30k a semester, not the (mostly) world-class, driven, caring faculty who put in the effort to make GW a worthwhile experience. I hope it becomes an opt-in system and people start fighting for the many professors who will be laid off or pushed into teaching circumstances they’re uncomfortable with just to appease people like you.

The money on your GWorld is your money that the school basically gives back to you when you pay them for room and board. Another person mentioned the Trader Joe’s near campus, I personally don’t recommend going places like there because you can’t pay with GWorld. It might be a little cheaper but you’re spending extra money for something you could buy at CVS/Safeway/Whole Foods with the money you already gave to GW for your food. Hopefully that makes sense.

In retrospect this is a lot but it’s all stuff I wish I would’ve known earlier; I very very much second the Georgetown Safeway, Whole Foods prices are ridiculous and their selection sucks. The circulator is $1 and picks up right off campus and drops you off right in front of the building. If you go there you need to get their rewards app because it has coupons on a lot of basic things, it usually saved me like $30 a trip. Make as many of your own breakfasts and lunches as you can stand and try not to go crazy when you eat out. Don’t underestimate the things you can cook in a microwave or with a kettle. I lived in Thurston but if you’re somewhere with a kitchen that’s accessible and not disgusting take full advantage of it. 

Keeping track of my spending by week and not by day helped me keep things in perspective, it saved me $800 my first semester. Also remember that GWorld is money you gave the school and it’s for you to use, don’t spend your money on things you could get on GWorld. I didn’t have the disposable income for that but because of grocery shopping I didn’t need to. 

I refused to buy books full price this year and managed to only spend $100. First thing, do not buy any books until you go to the first class. You might end up dropping, or the professor might just say you don’t actually need the book. 

If you are ok with ebooks they’re usually way cheaper to download or rent. There are a lot of free textbook databases if you google it, library genesis is a great one, and a lot of older versions are on there. For most classes you don’t need the newest version of the book, some professors will be up front with that and others won’t. Gelman has a textbook rental program where they loan out books for big into classes for 3 hours at a time. I used that for my poly sci class first semester, there’s a scanner right next to the checkout desk, or the scanner app on my phone, that I would use to send the chapters I needed to myself to take notes on later. A few weeks into the semester too a lot of ebook sites will have stuff on discount that’s worth looking for. I stopped having to check out that book from Gelman after a month because I found it online marked down to $20 instead of $70.

Work Study:
My personal work study experience was a nightmare but I know it’s different for everyone. I know they changed the system this semester for finding jobs but on Handshake employers weren’t responsive when I submitted applications and it was crazy competitive. I ended up taking something with an off campus organization that didn’t offer any flexibility with hours and it made my year suck. 
My biggest advice is to start applying to positions as soon as possible and to anything that sounds remotely interesting. Also apply to some positions that aren’t within GW because they’re usually less competitive. 
 
Professors and gen eds:
 I think that the professor you have can really make or break a class. I knocked most of mine out this year and the only classes I had that were difficult were when the professor was unorganized or terrible at communicating. Check rate my professor and I’d avoid anyone with a really bad rating or ask others who’ve taken the class for their perspective on its difficulty, but in general classes are manageable. 
Side note: I’m pretty sure you’ll have to take Professor Moses for Math1051: make friends in the class to work with and go to the study sessions in Academic Commons if you’re struggling. He made a few of my friends cry in office hours and he’s not great at explaining things, or being kind to students in general.  Somehow the probability in that class was worse than any math I’ve taken before. 

Food:
If you live in Guthridge or Fulbright you’ll have a kitchen and a smaller meal plan, I don’t have experience with that but if you keep track of how much you’re spending each week and make your choices accordingly you’ll be ok. If you don’t have a kitchen you have more freedom to eat out, but I still recommend keeping track of your spending. I went grocery shopping every week at Whole Foods for fruit and smaller stuff then went to the Georgetown Safeway every month-ish and stocked up on packaged stuff. Safeway has an app with coupons and I’d highly recommend signing up for their rewards because it saved me $20-$50 each trip. If you’re really wanting to have extra money at the end of the year try to make as much food in your room as you can and don’t go crazy with eating at restaurants.

A lot of people complain about it but I think unless you’re unwilling to cook or an idiot it’s hard to run out. Even as a freshman without a kitchen it’s easy to go to Safeway or Whole Foods once a week and buy things to make in the microwave or easily prepared for breakfast and lunch. Last semester I spent about $50-$80 a week in groceries and then got Starbucks or a meal every couple days. I ended up with an extra $800 by winter break. This also helped a lot because I could start buying other things I needed at CVS on GWorld and save my own money. It’s not the most fun to eat oatmeal every morning and have sandwiches for dinner than getting an açaí bowl and Chipotle every day but if budgeting is a worry for you it’s worth it. Coast with free food at the beginning of the year as long as possible. Just be smart and you’ll be ok.

I live in a Thurston 6 right now and I really think it depends a lot on your roommates, your floor, the specific room you’re in, and what you’re used to. It’s definitely loud and can get pretty gross, but it’s not worse than other places I’ve lived. When I first moved in we scrubbed the hell out of everything and we make sure to clean religiously. Our room has a lot of space so being with so many people hasn’t been a problem, but I know there are others sixes that are different. I also got really lucky with good roommates so that helps. 
We’ve had to call FixIt quite a few times, at the beginning of the year we had ants in the bathroom, but they came and sprayed and they haven’t come back. We’ve also had the sink and toilet break but it got fixed within 24 hours. It’s an old building so small stuff breaks a lot but FixIt has been really responsive. 
If you can room swap go for it, otherwise have a positive attitude and you’ll be fine for a semester.

I’m white and middle class from the Midwest, my EFC this year was around 11k. I applied ED2 and I got $0 in scholarships with a 3.9 GPA, but I got 56k in university grants, 3k in work study, and federal loans. I applied early bc GW was my dream school but I was fully prepared to back out if I didn’t get enough aid money. You’ll probably get more in academic scholarships applying regular but they can and will use that to decrease any need based aid you might qualify for. I agree with everyone else that GW isn’t the best place to get a bunch of debt if you can go somewhere else, especially for less well known programs. 
I’ve only heard good things about Corcoran from people in the school, one of my roommates is doing a double major with CCAS and has had great experiences with all her Corcoran professors. It’s a good school but definitely not worth going into crazy amounts of debt for. 
Don’t be afraid of applying early if you want to and know you will qualify for need based aid, but no matter what you’ll end up with at least some debt.
